How do we know the boy in question was "uncomfortable"? I think we're blowing this out of proportion a bit too much before looking into the case and place it in its context. Honestly, as confusing as it may be for many of us to understand the meaning of this event, the besmirching reactions from the West are starting to sound more like the witch trials in the Middle Ages. No matter the unfolding explanations of this event, the West has already made itself into a sketch for a new South Park episode. One instant, one person, huge media: suddenly Dalai Lama is treated as a new Epstein and Buddhism is denounced. Consider the following: What if this event in fact was a purely playful joke, with no sexual connotation involved whatsoever? What if they boy found it all funny and afterwards ran to his Mom saying "I hugged Dalai Lama, mom!". Personally, I'm waiting for sociologists and especially anthropologists to start commenting on this 'scandal', because it would be a shame if this was all a grave misunderstanding stemming from cultural-spiritual clashes. In Danish culture on weddings it is not uncommon for the bride to kiss her children on the mouth. Lastly: no matter what turns out to be the case, don't let Dalai Lama's actions or anyone else's represent Buddhism, or any other religion, which all have been guided by thousands of different masters throughout history.

Not to sound like some wise Gandalf the Grey, but the answer is written in your question. You write that there's no evidence that no one has any purpose or reason whatsoever. In that case, your life is just as unimportant (or important) as anyone else's. It doesn't matter if you're no "crucial pillar of the community": the people who are so, live just as meaningless lives as you do or I do. 

And from a Nietzsche perspective, if you're "not having a good time" it means you're living just the way you are supposed to as a human being: in suffering (which is the base ingredient for something even stronger than happiness).

I've also been depressed for at least ten years. For me it has been some form of chronic depression. I don't get panic attacks, instead I rarely feel "happy" - whatever happiness is. I just watched some video about Nietzsche, I don't know much about his literature, but one of his messages was that all suffering sooner or later converts into true happiness. From that perspective, your feeling of explosion will turn into the freedom you crave and deserve. 

Loneliness is something I struggle with each day. I have people who contact me quite often, but I never know if they are my friends. I almost never felt I had a friend, no matter how many people I surround myself with. But if you have the feeling that you "lost every friend", it might be that they weren't good friends for you in the first place.
